summary: Lactase is an oral digestive enzyme supplement (beta-galactosidase, often derived from Aspergillus or Kluyveromyces) used to aid the digestion of lactose in people with lactase deficiency or lactose intolerance. Taken with the first bite of dairy-containing food, it breaks down lactose into the absorbable simple sugars glucose and galactose, preventing the bloating, gas, cramping, and diarrhea that occur when undigested lactose reaches the colon. It is taken at the start of a lactose-containing meal, and the amount is adjusted to the lactose content of the food and individual tolerance. Because it acts locally in the gut and is not meaningfully absorbed, it is well tolerated. NOTE: lactase is marketed as an over-the-counter dietary supplement/enzyme aid, not as an FDA-approved drug; it does not treat the underlying galactosemia or other conditions.

moa: Lactase (beta-galactosidase) is the enzyme normally produced by the brush-border cells of the small intestine. It hydrolyzes the disaccharide lactose into its constituent monosaccharides, glucose and galactose, which are then absorbed across the intestinal mucosa. In lactase-deficient individuals, supplemental lactase taken with dairy performs this hydrolysis exogenously in the gut lumen, preventing undigested lactose from reaching the colon where bacterial fermentation produces gas and osmotic diarrhea. The enzyme acts locally and is itself digested as a protein.

preg: Lactase is considered safe in pregnancy. It acts locally within the gastrointestinal tract and is not meaningfully absorbed, so systemic exposure to the fetus is not expected. Use as needed for lactose-intolerance symptoms.
lact: Lactase is considered safe during breastfeeding. It is not systemically absorbed and does not enter breast milk in a way that would affect the infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment; lactase acts locally in the gut and is not renally eliminated.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

Timing is everything: take with the FIRST bite of dairy; taking it late markedly reduces benefit

missed: Lactase is taken only when consuming lactose-containing food. If you forget to take it before a dairy meal, taking it afterward is much less effective; simply take it with your next dairy-containing meal. There is no scheduled dose to make up.
overdose: Lactase has a very wide margin of safety, and overdose is not expected to cause harm because the enzyme acts locally and is digested as a protein. Excess may cause mild gastrointestinal discomfort. No specific treatment is required beyond supportive care.
